content_units: Best Laptop Fit for a CS Student

For a computer science student who codes daily, takes notes in class, and only occasionally edits photos,   Option C is the best overall fit  . It balances portability, enough performance, note-taking convenience, and solid value under your   USD 1,400   cap.
Portability, Longevity, and Value Comparison
Option   Portability   Longevity   Value   Best For

A     Excellent   — 1.24 kg, 13.6-inch, 18-hour battery   Good — 16 GB RAM and 512 GB SSD are still strong for CS workloads   Good if priced well, but lacks extra flexibility   Students who want maximum battery life and the lightest carry

B   Good — 1.55 kg is still manageable, but heavier; 10-hour battery is the weakest here     Excellent   — 32 GB RAM and 1 TB SSD give the most headroom for years   Strong on raw specs, but only if you need that power   Heavy multitasking, VMs, large datasets, more serious photo/editing work

C   Very good — 1.4 kg, 14-inch, 12-hour battery   Good to very good — 16 GB RAM/512 GB SSD should last well for most CS students     Best overall   — adds touchscreen + stylus without giving up portability   Coding, handwritten notes, diagrams, and light creative work
Option 1:   Option C     Best balance for coding, classes, and note-taking     Touchscreen + stylus adds real student value
Choose C
Option 2:   Option A     Best if battery life and lowest weight matter most     18-hour battery
Choose A
Option 3:   Option B     Best for maximum future-proofing and heavier workloads     32 GB RAM + 1 TB SSD
Choose B
Student-Focused Verdict
Why Option C wins
-   Programming:   16 GB RAM and 512 GB SSD are enough for most CS coursework, IDEs, browsers, Docker, and moderate multitasking.
-   Note-taking:   The   touchscreen and included stylus   are a major advantage for lectures, annotating PDFs, sketching system designs, and math-heavy classes.
-   Photo editing:   It is suitable for occasional editing, even if not as powerful as Option B.
-   Everyday carry:   At   1.4 kg  , it is still portable enough for commuting across campus.
-   Value:   You are getting a feature that directly improves student life, not just bigger specs on paper.
When Option A is better
Choose A if your top priorities are:
- The   lightest   laptop
- The   best battery life
- Mostly standard coding, writing, browsing, and classroom use
- You do   not   care much about handwriting or touchscreen notes
This is the most travel-friendly option, but it is less versatile for note-taking than C.
When Option B is better
Choose B if you expect to:
- Run multiple VMs or containers often
- Work with larger coding projects
- Keep many apps open all day
- Edit photos more seriously
- Want the most future-proof specs
Its downside is that it is the   heaviest   and has the   shortest battery life  , which matters a lot for campus use.
Budget Context

Given only the specs, I’m assuming   all three fit within your USD 1,400 cap  . If their prices are close,   Option C   gives the best student-centered value. If   Option B   is only slightly more expensive and you know you will run heavier workloads, it becomes the better long-term power pick.
